subject: Social Science
title: The Village Rules: Panchayati Raj
hook: How do villages govern themselves? Who makes decisions about water, schools, and roads?

characters.name: Ravi
characters.role: A 12-year-old from a village in Madhya Pradesh

characters.name: Lakshmi
characters.role: Ravi's friend whose mother is a Sarpanch (village leader)

slides.title: Grassroots Democracy - Rural Local Government
slides.storyContext: Ravi's village needs a new water pipeline, and a dispute has arisen between two families over land. Ravi watches as his village's Panchayat (council) calls a meeting. He sees how local democracy works—not in a distant capital, but right in his village.

slides.title: Panchayat Sammelan (Village Meeting)
slides.storyContext: Shri Yadav, the Sarpanch, rings the village bell. All adults gather under the banyan tree (or in the community hall). He asks: 'The school needs repairs, and the water tank is leaking. What should we do?' Farmers, shopkeepers, women, landless laborers—everyone speaks. After 2 hours of discussion, they vote and decide to repair the water tank first. Ravi realizes: this is democracy at its most basic level.

image.alt: Panchayat Sammelan (Village Meeting) — Grassroots Democracy - Rural Local Government

slides.title: What is Panchayati Raj? The Three-Tier System
slides.storyContext: Lakshmi's mother explains: 'Panchayati Raj means the rule of the Panchayat. In 1992, India made a law saying every village must have elected councils at three levels.'

points.label: Definition
points.text: Panchayati Raj (rule by Panchayat) is the system of village self-government in India. Every village has an elected Panchayat to govern locally.

points.label: Three tiers
points.text: Village Panchayat (smallest—one per village), Block Panchayat (one per 40-50 villages), and District Panchayat (one per district). Each tier is elected.

points.label: 73rd Amendment
points.text: In 1992, India's Constitution was amended to make local governance mandatory. No state could ignore local elections.

example.problem: A village with 1,000 people needs a school. Should (a) the national government decide, (b) the state government decide, or (c) the village Panchayat decide?
example.solution: (c) The village Panchayat should decide because they know their needs best. But they can get funding from state/national levels. Local governance is about decision-making power staying with the people.

slides.inSimpleWords: Panchayati Raj means villages rule themselves. They elect a council (Panchayat) to make local decisions.

slides.title: Structure of a Village Panchayat
slides.storyContext: Ravi learns that his village Panchayat has 7 members: a Sarpanch (leader), a Vice Sarpanch, and 5 Panchayat members. All are elected by the villagers.

points.label: Sarpanch
points.text: The elected chief/president of the Panchayat. Elected by villagers or by Panchayat members. Presides over meetings and implements decisions.

points.label: Vice Sarpanch
points.text: Second-in-command. Assists the Sarpanch and acts in his/her absence.

points.label: Panchayat members (Gram Sachiv)
points.text: Elected representatives. Their number varies by village size (usually 5-15). Each represents a ward (sub-area of the village).

points.label: Secretary (Lekhpal)
points.text: A government employee (not elected) who keeps records and helps the Panchayat.

example.problem: Lakshmi's mother is running for Sarpanch. To be elected, she needs support from (a) the district collector, (b) the state government, or (c) the majority of villagers?
example.solution: (c) Villagers vote for the Sarpanch directly or Panchayat members vote for her to be Sarpanch. No bureaucrat can appoint her. This is democracy.

slides.inSimpleWords: A village Panchayat has a Sarpanch (leader), a Vice Sarpanch, and elected members. All are chosen by the village.

slides.title: Powers and Duties of the Panchayat
slides.storyContext: Shri Yadav, the Sarpanch, is busy. Yesterday he settled a dispute about a stolen goat; today he's deciding on the new school building's location; tomorrow he'll meet the block officer about the water project.

points.label: Development works
points.text: Building and maintaining roads, water tanks, drains, community centers, anganwadis (nutrition centers), and schools.

points.label: Dispute resolution
points.text: Settling minor disputes between villagers (land boundaries, property quarrels) without going to court.

points.label: Collection of local taxes
points.text: Collecting property tax and other local levies to fund village projects.

points.label: Social welfare
points.text: Organizing welfare programs for the poor, disabled, widows, and elderly. Managing ration cards, pensions.

points.label: Safety and sanitation
points.text: Ensuring clean water, waste management, vaccinations, and basic health camps.

example.problem: A Panchayat member stole public money. Can the Sarpanch punish him?
example.solution: The Sarpanch can suspend him and file a report to the police/state authorities. The Panchayat is not above the law. Corruption cases go to court.

slides.inSimpleWords: The Panchayat handles water, roads, schools, health, and local disputes. It's responsible for the village's well-being.

slides.title: Reservation for Women and SCs/STs
slides.storyContext: Ravi notices that in his Panchayat, one-third of the seats are reserved for women. His friend Lakshmi's mother could run for Sarpanch even in a male-dominated village. There are also reserved seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.

points.label: Women reservation
points.text: At least 1/3 of Panchayat seats (and often the Sarpanch post) are reserved for women. This ensures women's voices in decision-making.

points.label: SC/ST reservation
points.text: Seats are reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes proportional to their population. This prevents discrimination.

points.label: Why it matters
points.text: Without reservation, upper-caste men would dominate. Reservation ensures the village hears from the poorest and most marginalized.

example.problem: A village has 7 Panchayat seats. How should they be divided?
example.solution: At least 2-3 for women (1/3), then some for SC/ST candidates (based on local SC/ST population), and the rest open. If 30% are SC/ST, 2-3 seats go to SC/ST candidates. This ensures representation.

slides.inSimpleWords: Panchayats must give seats to women and members of SC/ST communities. This way, everyone in the village has a voice.

slides.title: How Funds Flow to Villages: Budget and Sources
slides.storyContext: Ravi asks: 'Where does the money come from to fix roads and build schools?' His uncle, who works in the block office, explains: 'From your own village taxes, plus grants from the state and national governments.'

points.label: Local taxes and levies
points.text: The Panchayat collects property tax, water charges, and market fees from villagers.

points.label: State allocation
points.text: The state government gives grants to Panchayats under schemes like NRLM (National Rural Livelihoods Mission) and MNREGA (rural jobs).

points.label: National government funds
points.text: Schemes like Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (rural roads) and Jal Jeevan Mission (water) provide central funds.

points.label: Transparency
points.text: The Panchayat must publish its budget publicly (on the village notice board). Anyone can audit the accounts.

example.problem: Ravi's village needed a water tank (cost: 5 lakhs rupees). The village tax brought in only 1 lakh. How did they build it?
example.solution: The Panchayat applied for a state grant (Jal Jeevan Mission provides 90% subsidy). Villagers contributed 1 lakh, and the state gave 4 lakhs. The tank was built and villagers owned it together.

slides.inSimpleWords: Villages get money from local taxes and government grants. The Panchayat plans a budget and spends money on village needs.

slides.title: Challenge: Design a Village Budget
slides.storyContext: Ravi's Panchayat has collected 10 lakhs rupees this year from local taxes and got a 20 lakh grant from the state. With 30 lakhs total, the Sarpanch must decide: What should the money go to?

example.problem: Priority list: (1) Fix the broken water pipeline (8 lakhs), (2) Build an Anganwadi for nutrition (5 lakhs), (3) Improve the school (6 lakhs), (4) Repair roads (12 lakhs). Total needs: 31 lakhs, but budget is 30 lakhs. Decide on 3 priorities and explain why.
example.solution: One solution: (1) Fix water (8L—critical for health), (2) Road repairs (12L—affects everyone), (3) Anganwadi (5L—children's nutrition). Total: 25L. Defer school to next year. This prioritizes survival and daily life. Other solutions are valid if justified. This teaches budgeting and values.

slides.inSimpleWords: A Panchayat must choose which projects to fund. They must balance needs and limited money. Every choice affects the village.

slides.title: The Village Rules
slides.storyContext: Ravi has learned that Panchayati Raj is democracy at its most authentic form. The villagers are not distant from power—they ARE the power.

points.text: Panchayati Raj means villages govern themselves through elected councils.
Three tiers: Village Panchayat, Block Panchayat, District Panchayat.
The Panchayat handles water, roads, schools, health, and local disputes.
Women and SC/ST members have reserved seats to ensure equal voice.
Villages get funds from local taxes and state/national grants.
The Panchayat budget is public—anyone can check how money is spent.

slides.inSimpleWords: In Panchayati Raj, villagers are in charge. They elect leaders and decide what their village needs.

subject: Social Science
title: The City Runs: Urban Local Bodies
hook: How do cities govern themselves? Who fixes roads, collects garbage, and runs schools in a city?

characters.name: Isha
characters.role: A 12-year-old from a mid-sized city in Karnataka

characters.name: Isha's mother
characters.role: A city employee working in the municipal corporation

characters.name: Councillor Deepak
characters.role: An elected ward councillor in the city

slides.title: Grassroots Democracy - Urban Local Government
slides.storyContext: Isha lives in a city of 2 million people. Every morning, she sees garbage collectors, sweepers, and water tankers on the streets. She wonders: 'Who employs them? Who decides if a road gets fixed or a new park is built?' Her mother says: 'The Municipal Corporation (Nagar Nigam). It's the city's government.'

slides.title: The Ward Meeting
slides.storyContext: Isha attends a public meeting in her ward (neighborhood). Councillor Deepak asks residents: 'What are the top 3 problems in our ward?' People complain: 'The water supply fails twice a week.' 'Potholes on our street.' 'The street light outside the school is broken.' Deepak takes notes and says: 'I'll take these to the Municipal Corporation's budget meeting next month.' Isha sees: even in a big city, local democracy is real.

slides.title: Types of Urban Local Bodies (Municipalities)
slides.storyContext: Isha learns that India's cities are governed by three types of municipal bodies, depending on size and importance.

points.label: Nagar Nigam (Municipal Corporation)
points.text: For large cities (population above 10 lakhs). Examples: Mumbai, Delhi, Bangalore. Headed by a Mayor and has a large elected council.

points.label: Nagar Palika (Municipality)
points.text: For medium cities (1-10 lakhs population). Examples: Nagpur, Jaipur. Headed by a President/Mayor and a smaller council.

points.label: Nagar Panchayat (Town Council)
points.text: For small towns and growing areas. Headed by a Chairperson and has a small council. Transitional between village and city governance.

example.problem: Isha's city has 2 million people. Should it be governed by a Nagar Panchayat, Nagar Palika, or Nagar Nigam?
example.solution: A Nagar Nigam (Municipal Corporation) is best for such a large city. It has the most resources and departments to handle 2 million people's needs.

slides.inSimpleWords: Big cities have a Nagar Nigam, medium cities have a Nagar Palika, and small towns have a Nagar Panchayat. Each type is suited to different city sizes.

slides.title: Structure of a Municipal Corporation
slides.storyContext: Isha's mother works in the Municipal Corporation. She shows Isha the organization: a Mayor (elected leader), Councillors (elected representatives from wards), a Municipal Commissioner (top bureaucrat), and various departments.

points.label: Mayor (elected)
points.text: The elected head of the corporation. Symbolic role (like the President) + presides over council meetings. Elected by voters or by councillors.

points.label: Deputy Mayor (elected)
points.text: Assists the Mayor. Often from a specific community or gender to ensure representation.

points.label: Councillors (elected)
points.text: Elected from wards (subdivisions of the city). Each ward (30,000-50,000 people) elects 1-2 councillors. They represent ward interests in the council.

points.label: Municipal Commissioner (appointed bureaucrat)
points.text: The top official, NOT elected. Responsible for day-to-day operations: hiring staff, collecting taxes, awarding contracts.

example.problem: Isha's ward councillor promises to fix all roads. But the Mayor says only 50% can be repaired. Who has power?
example.solution: The Mayor and Commissioner have more power. The councillor represents the ward, but the corporation's budget and resources are managed by the Mayor and Commissioner. The councillor must convince them in council meetings.

slides.inSimpleWords: A city has elected leaders (Mayor, Councillors) and a top bureaucrat (Commissioner). Elected leaders make policy; the Commissioner runs day-to-day operations.

slides.title: Functions of Urban Local Bodies: The Services They Provide
slides.storyContext: Isha's mother lists what the corporation does: water supply, garbage collection, sewerage, roads, street lights, property registration, building permits, and vaccination camps.

points.label: Water and sanitation
points.text: Supplying drinking water, managing sewerage systems, drains, and ensuring public toilets.

points.label: Solid waste management
points.text: Collecting garbage, street cleaning, composting, and landfill management.

points.label: Public health
points.text: Running vaccination camps, health clinics, maternity centers, and disease control programs.

points.label: Roads and transport
points.text: Building and maintaining roads, street lights, public buses, parking, and traffic management.

points.label: Planning and permits
points.text: Granting building permits, planning new residential areas, ensuring city beautification.

points.label: Social welfare
points.text: Running schools, community centers, public libraries, markets, and welfare programs for the poor.

example.problem: During monsoon, Isha's street floods with sewage. Who should fix it?
example.solution: The Municipal Corporation (sewerage and drainage department). If they delay, Isha's ward councillor can raise it in the council or approach the Commissioner. The corporation is accountable to residents.

slides.inSimpleWords: The city's municipal body provides water, removes garbage, repairs roads, runs hospitals, and maintains everything that makes city life possible.

slides.title: Ward System and Representation
slides.storyContext: Isha's city is divided into 100 wards. Her ward (Ward 45) has about 40,000 people. Every 5 years, they elect 2 councillors—1 from a general seat and 1 from a reserved seat (women, SC, or ST).

points.label: Ward definition
points.text: A city is divided into wards (geographic subdivisions). Each ward elects 1-2 councillors who represent its interests.

points.label: Representation formula
points.text: Usually: 1 councillor per 30,000-50,000 people. A city of 2 million might have 40-50 wards.

points.label: Reserved seats
points.text: Like Panchayats, municipal wards have reserved seats for women (1/3 of all seats), SCs, and STs (proportional to population).

points.label: Councillor's role
points.text: Represent the ward in council, bring grievances, vote on city budget, and advocate for local projects.

example.problem: Ward 45 has 40,000 people but elects 2 councillors. How do they represent everyone?
example.solution: The 2 councillors meet with residents regularly, listen to complaints, and raise them in the city council. They also hold public meetings (like Panchayat meetings) to discuss ward problems.

slides.inSimpleWords: A city is divided into wards. Each ward elects councillors to represent their interests in the city council.

slides.title: Finance: How Cities Earn and Spend Money
slides.storyContext: Isha's mother explains: 'The city needs money for water pipes, garbage trucks, salaries. Where does it come from?'

points.label: Property tax
points.text: Charged on every building in the city (4-10% of property value annually). Largest source of city revenue.

points.label: Water and sewerage charges
points.text: Residents pay for water and sewerage. Commerces pay more for large consumption.

points.label: Market and parking fees
points.text: Vendors in city markets pay rent; vehicles pay parking fees.

points.label: State and national grants
points.text: State government provides grants; national schemes like AMRUT (water and sanitation) provide central funding.

points.label: Budget transparency
points.text: The city budget is published. The council debates and approves it. Anyone can demand an audit.

example.problem: Isha's property tax is 5,000 rupees/year. The city collects 50 crores from 1 million properties. But the budget shows 200 crores needed (water supply costs 80 crores, garbage costs 30 crores, salaries 60 crores, roads 30 crores). Where does the extra money come from?
example.solution: Water and sewerage charges (30 crores), market fees (20 crores), state grants (40 crores), and borrowing/bonds. The city must plan carefully.

slides.inSimpleWords: Cities earn money from property tax, water charges, market fees, and government grants. The budget must balance income and spending.

slides.title: Challenge: A Councillor's Dilemma
slides.storyContext: Councillor Deepak has a limited fund (2 crores) for his ward this year. He has 5 urgent demands from residents: (1) Fix 10 km of broken roads (1.5 crores), (2) Install 50 new street lights (50 lakhs), (3) Build a community health center (1 crore), (4) Improve the school building (75 lakhs), (5) Repair the old park (50 lakhs). Total: 3.75 crores. He can only choose 2-3. What should he prioritize?

example.problem: Which 2-3 projects should Councillor Deepak fund from 2 crores?
example.solution: One answer: (1) Road repairs (1.5 crores—affects traffic and commerce), (2) Street lights (50 lakhs—safety issue). Defer health center and school. Another answer: (3) Health center (1 crore—critical for poor) + (2) Street lights (50 lakhs) + small portions of roads. Justify your choice based on urgency and impact. This teaches real governance trade-offs.

slides.inSimpleWords: A city councillor must choose which projects to fund. Like the Panchayat, there's limited money and unlimited needs. Choices reflect values.

slides.title: The City Runs
slides.storyContext: Isha now realizes: cities are complex, but they're still democratic. Elected councillors, transparent budgets, and public meetings ensure residents have a voice.

points.text: Three types of urban local bodies: Nagar Nigam (big cities), Nagar Palika (medium cities), Nagar Panchayat (towns).
Cities are divided into wards. Each ward elects councillors to represent residents.
A Mayor heads the corporation; a Commissioner handles day-to-day operations.
Urban bodies provide water, garbage collection, roads, health, and social services.
Cities earn money from property tax, water charges, market fees, and government grants.
Urban local democracy ensures residents have a voice in city decisions.

slides.inSimpleWords: Cities are governed by elected councillors and professional administrators. Together, they provide water, roads, health, and safety to millions of residents.

subject: Social Science
title: Work Feeds the World: Understanding Labor
hook: Why does work matter? What does a farmer, a teacher, or a builder contribute to society?

characters.name: Mohan
characters.role: A 12-year-old from a farming family in Punjab

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: His friend whose father is a doctor

characters.name: Grandmother Savitri
characters.role: A retired schoolteacher who now does community work

slides.title: The Value of Work
slides.storyContext: Mohan watches his father wake at dawn to work in the fields. Priya's father works long hours in a hospital. Grandmother Savitri, retired from teaching, now volunteers in the village school. Mohan wonders: 'Why do people work? Is farming less important than being a doctor? Is volunteer work real work?'

slides.title: Where Does Your Food Come From?
slides.storyContext: Grandmother Savitri asks the children: 'Close your eyes. Imagine a day without food, without clothes, without a house, without schools, hospitals, or roads. Who made all this?' 'Farmers grow food,' says Mohan. 'Tailors make clothes,' says Priya. 'Builders construct houses,' adds Mohan. 'And teachers educate children,' finishes Savitri. Every piece of the world is built by someone's labor. Every job matters.

image.alt: Where Does Your Food Come From? — The Value of Work

slides.title: What is Work? Paid and Unpaid Work
slides.storyContext: Grandmother Savitri teaches: 'Work is not just jobs that pay money. Work is any effort that produces something useful.'

points.label: Paid work (employment)
points.text: Work done for wages: farming, teaching, driving, nursing, engineering, shopkeeping. The person receives money in exchange.

points.label: Unpaid work
points.text: Work done without direct payment: cooking at home, caring for children, washing clothes, gardening for family, community volunteer work.

points.label: Why unpaid work matters
points.text: Families survive on unpaid work. Women do most unpaid work globally. Without it, society collapses.

points.label: Work has dignity
points.text: No job is shameful. A cleaner's work is as valuable as a CEO's work. Both contribute to society.

example.problem: Mohan's mother cooks for the family daily (5 hours) but earns no money. Is she working?
example.solution: Yes, absolutely. She's doing crucial unpaid work. If this work were paid, a family would spend 15,000+ rupees monthly on a cook. Her unpaid labor saves the family and sustains it. Unpaid work is still work.

slides.inSimpleWords: Work includes both paid jobs and unpaid household tasks. Both are valuable. Cooking, childcare, and housework are real work.

slides.title: Types of Work: Primary, Secondary, Tertiary Sectors
slides.storyContext: Grandmother Savitri explains that all work falls into three categories based on what the worker does.

points.label: Primary sector (extractive industries)
points.text: Directly extracting from nature: farming, fishing, mining, forestry. Workers: farmers, fishermen, miners. About 50% of Indians work in this sector.

points.label: Secondary sector (manufacturing)
points.text: Converting raw materials into finished products: factories making clothes, cars, furniture, steel. Workers: factory workers, artisans, construction workers.

points.label: Tertiary sector (services)
points.text: Providing services: teaching, healthcare, transportation, shops, banks, government work. Workers: teachers, doctors, drivers, shopkeepers, police.

example.problem: Mohan's village has: (1) a rice farmer (primary), (2) a rice mill (secondary), (3) a grain shop (tertiary). Which worker depends on which?
example.solution: The farmer grows rice (primary). The mill owner buys rice and processes it (secondary). The shop sells processed rice (tertiary). The farmer enables the mill, which enables the shop. All three sectors are interdependent.

slides.inSimpleWords: Work is divided into three types: Primary (farming, fishing), Secondary (manufacturing), Tertiary (services like teaching, healthcare, shops).

slides.title: Skilled and Unskilled Work; Organized and Unorganized Sectors
slides.storyContext: Mohan learns that jobs differ not just in type but in skill level, stability, and benefits.

points.label: Skilled work
points.text: Requires training or education: doctor, engineer, teacher, electrician, plumber, accountant. Usually better pay and conditions.

points.label: Unskilled work
points.text: Minimal training required: farm laborer, construction worker, street sweeper, rickshaw puller. Often lower pay and harder conditions.

points.label: Organized sector
points.text: Formal employment with contracts, fixed salary, benefits (health insurance, pension), and legal protection. Examples: government job, factory worker, teacher.

points.label: Unorganized sector
points.text: No formal contract; no benefits; work is irregular and income uncertain. Examples: street vendor, daily laborer, domestic worker. About 90% of Indians work in this sector.

example.problem: Two workers: (1) A teacher with a government contract, salary, and health insurance. (2) A street vendor who works 12 hours but has no contract and no insurance. Are they both workers?
example.solution: Yes, both are workers. But the teacher has more security. The vendor is vulnerable—one illness or injury means no income. This inequality is a major issue in India. Better wages and protections for unorganized workers are a policy goal.

slides.inSimpleWords: Some jobs are skilled (doctor, engineer) and others are unskilled (laborer). Some jobs have contracts and benefits (organized), and others don't (unorganized).

slides.title: Child Labor: Why Kids Should Study, Not Work
slides.storyContext: Grandmother Savitri talks about a difficult topic: 'In poor families, children work in fields or factories instead of going to school. This is child labor. It's illegal and cruel.'

points.label: What is child labor?
points.text: Work done by children below 18 that prevents them from attending school or harms their health. Examples: mining, factory work, domestic servitude, sex trafficking.

points.label: Why it's wrong
points.text: Child labor steals a child's future. Without education, they stay poor and unskilled. It's exploitation.

points.label: Legal protection
points.text: Indian law (Child Labour Prohibition and Regulation Act) bans child labor. Every child has the RIGHT to education, not work.

points.label: Root cause
points.text: Poverty forces families to send children to work. Fixing child labor requires ensuring parents earn enough and families can afford school.

example.problem: A poor family needs money. Their 14-year-old son can earn 5,000/month working in a factory. Should he work or study?
example.solution: He SHOULD study. The government provides free education (Right to Free and Compulsory Education Act). The family should apply for financial aid, scholarships, or MNREGA work (adult rural jobs). The son's future is more important than immediate income.

slides.inSimpleWords: Children should study, not work. Child labor is illegal in India because every child deserves an education and a childhood.

slides.title: Gender and Work: Why Women Are Undervalued
slides.storyContext: Priya's mother is a doctor but earns less than her male colleagues. Mohan's mother does all the housework but is called 'just a housewife.' Grandmother Savitri explains: 'Society undervalues women's work.'

points.label: The wage gap
points.text: Women are paid less than men for the same work (gender wage gap). On average, Indian women earn 20-30% less than men.

points.label: Unpaid work burden
points.text: Women do 80% of unpaid household work (cooking, childcare, washing) while also working outside. Men do half.

points.label: Career barriers
points.text: Women face discrimination in hiring, promotion, and leadership roles. They're pushed toward 'suitable' jobs (nursing, teaching).

points.label: Solutions
points.text: Equal pay laws, paid maternity leave, flexible work hours, women's education, and cultural respect for women's work.

example.problem: Priya's parents both work as doctors. Her father earns 1 lakh/month, her mother earns 85,000/month for the same job. Why?
example.solution: Discrimination based on gender. By law, this is illegal (Equal Remuneration Act, 1976). Priya's mother should report this to the labor department. Businesses that discriminate on pay face fines and penalties.

slides.inSimpleWords: Women are often paid less than men for the same work. Women also do most unpaid housework. This is unfair and must change.

slides.title: The Dignity of Labor: Changing Attitudes Toward Work
slides.storyContext: In India, manual labor (farming, cleaning, construction) is often looked down upon. Grandmother Savitri challenges this: 'Every job has dignity. A farmer feeds millions. A sweeper keeps cities clean. These workers deserve respect.'

points.label: Historical caste system
points.text: In ancient India, castes were birth-based occupation groups. Certain jobs (like cleaning) were considered 'untouchable.' This legacy persists.

points.label: Modern prejudice
points.text: Today, manual workers face discrimination in education, employment, and social status. Families pressure children to avoid 'low-status' jobs.

points.label: Reality check
points.text: Farmers provide food. Cleaners prevent disease. Builders create infrastructure. Drivers transport people. Each job is essential.

points.label: Respect for all workers
points.text: A true democracy respects all workers equally. Dignity comes from honest work, not the type of work.

example.problem: A student's father is a street sweeper. At school, a classmate says, 'Your father has a dirty job.' How should the student respond?
example.solution: The student should be proud. Street sweepers keep cities clean and prevent disease. This is essential work. The classmate's ignorance is the problem, not the father's job. In a democracy, all jobs deserve respect.

slides.inSimpleWords: All work has value and dignity. A farmer, a teacher, a cleaner, a builder—all are equally important to society.

slides.title: Work Feeds the World
slides.storyContext: Mohan now understands: every person's work sustains society. From the farmer to the teacher to his grandmother's volunteer work—all matter.

points.text: Work is any effort that produces value: paid jobs or unpaid household work.
Three sectors: Primary (farming, fishing), Secondary (manufacturing), Tertiary (services).
Jobs are skilled or unskilled; organized (with contracts) or unorganized (irregular).
Child labor is illegal. Children have the right to education, not work.
Women face wage gaps and unequal treatment in work. This must change.
All work has dignity. Every worker deserves respect.

slides.inSimpleWords: Work is how society sustains itself. Every person's labor contributes. Farmers, teachers, doctors, cleaners—all are essential.
